text: His name was Alexander. In 326 B.C.E. he crossed into the Punjab. On the banks of the Jaelum
River a local king called Porus was waiting with something the Greeks had rarely faced
– war elephants. Keep those elephants in mind. Alexander won. And the Greek writers
tell a famous story about what came next.
How do you wish to be treated?
Like a king.
Sir, he lost.
Fair.
Keep your kingdom.
Then Alexander pushed east to the river Bias,
and there his army simply stopped.
They had marched for eight years.
The monsoon rain wouldn't stop,
and they had heard what was waiting beyond the river,
the Nanda kings of Magadha, with a gigantic army, thousands of elephants, and an even bigger
treasury. The soldiers refused to go any further. Alexander, who had never lost a battle, had
to turn back. He died in Babylon three years later at 32. But a young man in India had
been watching the Greeks very carefully, and he had a teacher with a grudge. The teacher
was a sharp, ruthless brahmin named Chanakya. He had been insulted at the Nanda court and
thrown out in front of everyone. So he untied the knot of his hair and swore he would not
tie it again until the Nandas were destroyed. That's the oath the old stories give him,
and he found exactly the weapon he needed, a young man named Chandragupta Maria.
Master, shall I bring a comb?
Not until the Nondus fall.
And how long might that be?
That depends on him.
